topic: The Pi-Collision Mystery: Physics Collisions and Numerical Discovery

sections.title: The Setup: The Elastic Collision Paradox
sections.content: Introduce the physical system: Two blocks of mass m1 and m2 sliding on a frictionless surface towards a wall. Define the conservation of momentum and kinetic energy as prerequisites for elastic collisions.
sections.example: A small block (mass 1kg) and a massive block (mass 100kg) moving toward a wall. The small block bounces off the wall and the large block repeatedly.

sections.title: Visualizing the Mapping: Momentum to Geometry
sections.content: Explain the phase space mapping. Instead of tracking spatial coordinates, plot velocities (v1, v2) as coordinates on a 2D plane. Show how each collision acts as a reflection vector against a circular arc.
sections.example: An animation showing the velocity vector point bouncing inside a circular boundary formed by the mass ratio m1/m2.

sections.title: The Bridge: Collision Counting and Pi
sections.content: Reveal the core mathematical insight: When the mass ratio m2/m1 = 100^n, the total number of collisions between the blocks and the wall equals the first n+1 digits of pi.
sections.example: A table showing m2/m1 = 1, 100, 10,000 resulting in 3, 31, and 314 collisions respectively.

sections.title: Application and Conclusion
sections.content: Synthesize the concept: Why does a physical collision mirror transcendental numbers? Conclude by demonstrating how simple mechanical rules can act as a 'computer' to calculate complex mathematical constants.
sections.example: A final visual of a robotic arm counting impacts until the digits of Pi are fully represented on a digital display.
